analysis.one_liner: Adds a Medicare benefit covering up to 20 hours a week of at-home help with daily living.
analysis.headline: The Medicare at Home Act was introduced in the House in August 2026 with one cosponsor and referred to two committees, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new Medicare benefit paying for home care workers to help older adults and people with disabilities with everyday tasks like bathing, dressing, and eating — care Medicare currently does not cover. It caps the benefit at 20 hours per week and requires a doctor to certify the person needs help. It pays for the new benefit by adjusting Medicare Part B premiums, and requires a payment rate that includes a wage floor for home care workers.
analysis.who_benefits: The bill's findings say more than 10 million Medicare beneficiaries need help with daily living and that Medicare does not cover long-term personal care at home, forcing families to pay out of pocket — often more than $60,000 a year — spend down into Medicaid, or go without care [S2]. The bill would cover up to 20 hours a week of help with activities of daily living and related household tasks, letting people stay in their homes instead of entering institutions, and easing pressure on unpaid family caregivers, whom the bill credits with providing over $1 trillion in unpaid care [S2]. Home care agencies and workers would gain a new Medicare revenue stream, with payment required to reflect a reasonable wage floor for home care workers [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Older adults and disabled Medicare beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: Medicare currently does not cover long-term personal care in the home, and more than 10 million beneficiaries need help with daily living activities; the bill adds home care services as a covered Part B benefit [S2].

Out-of-pocket home care costs more than $60,000 annually, and families otherwise spend down into Medicaid or forgo care; a capped Medicare benefit would let people remain at home and reduce avoidable hospitalizations [S2].

Eligibility is broad: anyone entitled to Medicare Part A or enrolled in Part B who is certified as needing help with at least two daily-living activities (or the equivalent mix) qualifies, though people already receiving duplicative home care through Medicaid are excluded to avoid double coverage [S2].
The bill requires the Medicare payment methodology for home care to reflect a reasonable wage floor for home care workers, a direct benefit to a workforce that is heavily female and low-paid [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The bill is financed by adjusting the monthly Medicare Part B premium to reflect the benefit's actuarial cost, subject to the standard premium subsidy schedule — so Medicare enrollees collectively pay through higher premiums, and the portion of premiums covered by the standard federal subsidy (about three-quarters of standard premium costs) is picked up by taxpayers. The Chief Actuary must report to Congress on the per-beneficiary premium impact within 180 days of enactment [S2]. All Part B enrollees would face somewhat higher premiums whether or not they use the benefit.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare enrollees via higher Part B premiums

drawbacks.text: The financing is a real cost, not free money: Part B premiums must rise to cover the benefit's actuarial cost, and the bill orders an official estimate of the per-beneficiary premium impact rather than capping it, so enrollees bear an open-ended, uncapped premium increase [S2].

The benefit is modest by design — capped at 20 hours per week and separate from Medicare's existing home health benefit — which would leave people with intensive needs still reliant on Medicaid or unpaid family care [S2].

A skeptical reader could note the bill does not create a dedicated funding source or offsets, so the true federal cost depends entirely on a payment methodology the Secretary would set later by regulation [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit addresses a large, well-documented gap: Medicare covers hospital and doctor care but not the daily help millions of beneficiaries need, and the alternative — $60,000+ a year out of pocket or spending down into Medicaid — is worse for families and often costlier for the health system overall. The main honest trade-off is that this is a genuine new entitlement financed by higher premiums on all Medicare enrollees and, through the standard subsidy, federal taxpayers, with the premium impact left to a future actuarial estimate rather than fixed in the bill. The 20-hour cap and Medicaid-coordination exclusion make it a modest benefit rather than a full long-term care program.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in August 2026, referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, and has had no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Debbie Dingell introduced the Medicare at Home Act in the House on August 3, 2026, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees [S1].
The bill has a single cosponsor, one House Democrat [S3].
The only actions in the record are introduction and the committee referrals; no hearing, markup, or floor vote has taken place, and the Congress runs through January 3, 2027 [S4].
The bill's own findings cite polling that 93 percent of adults agree Medicare should cover home care, and that most current beneficiaries either believe it already does or do not know [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has had to take a position: with one cosponsor and no committee action, the bill sits where most late-session, low-cosponsorship bills do. Home care agencies and workers gain nothing yet; Medicare beneficiaries continue paying for home care out of pocket or through Medicaid, as they do today.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — the bill sits idle in committee

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only support is from two Democrats (the sponsor and one cosponsor); no Republican has cosponsored and no votes have occurred, so the partisan shape is largely untested.

industries.industry: Home care agencies and home care workers
industries.note: The bill creates a new Medicare funding stream for home care delivered by enrolled agencies or individuals, with payment required to reflect a wage floor for home care workers. Beneficiaries gain access to care they currently pay for themselves or go without, so the industry's interest here runs alongside theirs — though routing the benefit through enrolled agencies makes those agencies the permanent channel for the new public benefit.

The bill adds home care services to traditional Medicare Part B; it is silent on how Medicare Advantage plans must cover it. Depending on later rules, insurers could face a new mandated benefit or gain flexibility in how they offer it.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and institutional long-term care providers
industries.note: A home care benefit is intended to help people stay out of institutions, which the bill's findings frame as reducing institutionalization; facilities that depend on residents who could otherwise remain home could see demand soften. The 20-hour cap limits how large that effect would be.

analysis.trajectory: With one cosponsor, no hearings, and roughly two months left in the session, the bill is very likely to die in committee when the 119th Congress ends on January 3, 2027, unless leadership elevates it — a fate typical of late-introduced, single-sponsor health bills. It would need to be reintroduced in the next Congress to have another chance.
